label: GPT-6.1 Sol

# Cup Day, or: bistro kitchens run on bar fridges and spite

Dear Jonno,

You can stop messaging me about the coolroom now. Here’s the whole thing, written down, because apparently moving to London means you’ve forgotten that when someone finishes a double, “what actually happened though” is not a small question.

Also, Mum, if you’re reading this, we’re all fine.

The coolroom compressor died sometime overnight between Monday and Tuesday. Found it at 6.40 on Cup Day morning, thermometer sitting on 11 degrees.

Eleven.

Lovely temperature for a walk. Less good for the contents of a commercial coolroom when you’ve got 140 people booked for a three-course set lunch.

I reckon you would’ve stood in the doorway for a solid minute doing that thing where you take your hat off and put it back on. Then you’d have said, “Nah, that’s fucked,” which would’ve been accurate but not especially useful. Although still more useful than Phil’s contribution, which was:

“Just make it work, mate.”

Cheers, Phil. Hadn’t considered that. I was going to put the bookings diary in the bin and get on the piss, but now you’ve said that, I’ll do lunch.

Raff was away, so I was running it. Which meant I got to be the bloke making the phone calls while also being the bloke everyone looked at after the phone calls.

Wally from Coldline couldn’t get there till Wednesday. Part had to come from Sydney. You know how it goes. There’s always a part, and it’s always in a different state to the thing it needs to be inside.

So that was that. Coolroom gone, Cup Day still happening.

We lost about eighteen hundred bucks of stock, mostly dairy and the duck legs. Properly painful throwing it out. There’s no funny version of looking at that much food and knowing it’s stuffed, so I’ll just say it was a shit start to the morning and move on.

Everything we could keep went into the two undercounters, the bar fridge and, thanks to Marta next door, half her walk-in.

You remember how much space there is in those undercounters. Enough for normal service, provided nobody buys anything and all the food is flat.

The bar fridge getting involved was particularly good. Nothing says “we have this under control” like the kitchen suddenly taking a professional interest in the available space beside the drinks.

Marta letting us use her walk-in is the only reason this isn’t a post about me changing careers. She has requested repayment in croissant credit. I owe her about three weeks of staff meal now, which is fair enough, although I suspect she’s going to remember this debt long after I reckon it’s paid.

Anyway, the bit you saw on my story was me and Benny taking thirty kilos of beef shin down the laneway on a milk crate trolley in the rain.

That was us doing logistics.

Thirty kilos of beef, two chefs, one trolley that had apparently been waiting years for a sufficiently inconvenient moment to lose a wheel.

Off it came.

I’d love to tell you we handled that with the calm professionalism you’d expect from two men entrusted with feeding the public, but you know both of us.

You would’ve lost your mind. Old Jonno might’ve helped. London Jonno would’ve stood under an awning telling us this sort of thing doesn’t happen at whatever place you’re paying twenty-six quid for lunch now.

You’ve been gone since February and I can already picture the face. Bit concerned. Bit cold. Wondering whether there’s someone we can call.

There was, mate. We called him. He was coming Wednesday.

Meanwhile Kev went to the servo and came back with fourteen bags of ice for the old esky.

Fourteen bags.

The servo bloke asked if we were having a party.

I hope Kev said yes. Easier than explaining that a bistro full of adults was being held together by ice, borrowed refrigeration and Phil’s belief in us.

And then, because bookings don’t disappear just because you’ve had an interesting morning, we had to do lunch.

One hundred and forty covers. Set menu. Three courses.

This is the bit that’s annoying to explain, because after all that, it was honestly the best service we did all year.

Everyone was locked in. Benny, Kev, all of us. Nobody needed a big speech. We knew what we had to get through, and there wasn’t much point carrying on about the coolroom when we still had a dining room to feed.

You know those services where you can feel everyone paying attention? No chasing people, no asking the same thing three times. Just people hearing each other and getting on with it.

It was one of those.

Obviously, we still had to 86 the panna cotta at 12.15.

Which is a lovely time to lose a dessert on a three-course set menu. Really lets you settle into lunch.

So dessert became “affogato with whatever”.

Not necessarily the wording you’d choose for the menu, but an honest description of where we were at.

And people loved it. More, possibly, than they would’ve loved the panna cotta. Which I found personally offensive after the morning we’d had. You spend all that time planning a menu and apparently what everyone actually wants is for you to run out of something and give them coffee.

I’m pleased they were happy. I just don’t want them getting the idea this is how we normally develop dishes.

Best comment of the day came from a lady on table nine. She’d seen me and Benny out the window with the beef.

Asked if it was “free range from the laneway”.

Fair play to her. That’s a good line. I’d have preferred her not to have witnessed our meat transport operation, but if you’re going to watch two blokes fight a broken trolley in the rain, you’re entitled to a question.

I know you’ll be furious you weren’t there to hear it. You’d have repeated it every time beef came on the menu for the next eighteen months. Probably written it on my prep list.

The other thing you need to know is that my horse in the sweep was called Ice Cold Lad.

I am not making that up.

On the day our coolroom died, I drew Ice Cold Lad.

Came second last.

Couldn’t even win enough to put a dent in the dairy. The universe had already got a pretty decent laugh out of us by then, but apparently it wanted one more.

So there you go. That’s what happened with the coolroom.

Eighteen hundred bucks in the bin. Half the kitchen living next door. Beef shin down the laneway. Fourteen bags of servo ice. Panna cotta off, affogato on. A woman on table nine absolutely getting us. Best service of the year, somehow.

I’m not going to make it into a whole thing about resilience. I’d have preferred a working fridge. We all would’ve had a much nicer morning if the compressor had simply continued compressing.

But I was pretty pleased with everyone by the end of it. We got lunch out, people had a good time, and now I can laugh about the wheel coming off instead of just staring at Benny.

Bistro kitchens run on bar fridges and spite. You knew that before you went overseas and got soft.

Anyway, next time you ask what you’re missing back here, I’ll send you this. You missed a very good service and several excellent opportunities to call me a dickhead. I missed having you there to push the trolley.

Come home ya flog.
